INSTRUCTIONS:
1. TARGETED THREAD ANALYSIS: Focus your analysis primarily on the MOST RECENT (top-level) email AND the IMMEDIATELY FORWARDED/REPLIED-TO email (the second email in the chain).
2. "KEEP" DECISION: You MUST return "keep" ONLY IF the Data Subject:
   - Is a Sender, Recipient, CC, or BCC of the top-level email OR the immediately forwarded/replied-to email.
   - Is explicitly discussed or mentioned by name in the newly written body text of the top-level email.
3. IMMEDIATE FORWARD/REPLY CONTEXT: If the Data Subject is the sender/recipient of a message that was forwarded by someone else to a third-party, you MUST keep both the original message AND the forwarded message.
   - Case Study: John (Subject) sends an email to Jane. Jane forwards John's email to Pedro. Pedro replies to Jane adding Sandra.
   - Analysis: In this scenario, keep the original message John sent to Jane, and the email Jane forwarded to Pedro (as it contains the direct communication from the Subject). Discard subsequent emails where the Subject's message is no longer actively discussed.
   - Chronological Order Warning: Outlook puts newer messages first. This means the Subject's original forwarded message will appear near the bottom of the raw text block. Scan the entire document carefully to locate it.
4. "DISCARD" DECISION (THREAD DECAY): You MUST return "discard" if the Data Subject's only appearance is deep in a large email chain (e.g. message 3, 4, 5+ in the thread history) and they are no longer an active participant in the recent correspondence.
5. NESTED EMAIL ATTACHMENTS (RECURSIVE CARRIERS): If the top-level email is unrelated but contains an attached email (.eml/.msg file) that matches the KEEP criteria, you MUST mark both the attached email AND the parent carrier email as "keep".
   - Case Study: Anne sends an email to Bob. Anne's email contains an attached email from the Subject to Carlos.
   - Analysis: Keep the attached email because the Subject is a participant. Keep Anne's email because it is the physical carrier of the attachment and must be preserved to allow extraction.
6. OUTPUT FORMAT: You must return ONLY a raw JSON object. Do not wrap the output in markdown code blocks (```json). Do not add conversational text.
Format exactly like this: {"decision": "keep" | "discard", "reason": "Brief justification."}

Stated reasons for my stress included that "I do not believe that the level of control that Gramercy appears to exert over the firm's governance allows the firm to act in the interests of all Claimants." That letter referred to the amount of effort I have put into working for the firm. It also referred at paragraph 15 to correspondence setting out governance and regulatory concerns: emails from my colleagues and me dated 8 September 2025 (11:23) and 4 September 2025 (09:19), and the letters attached to the email from Céline Barnwell on 5 September 2025, including but not limited to the execution and performance of the G3 credit agreement. No firm email or communication was sent about the policy's upload, introduction or terms.- The firm's position is that that policy upload amounted to a unilateral change to the terms of my employment contract, without notice or consent.- I was not told that the firm believed that the terms of my employment contract had been unilaterally changed.- 17-27 November: I led the PCD trial for PG, attending Court every day and with conduct of the case for PG.  Ben Croft (Leigh Day partner leading PCD for LD) was unwell and only attended Court for two days, so in practice I was the most senior Lead Solicitor in Court with carriage of the case.  The responsibility was serious, and I took it seriously.  At the same time I worked on a handover of the PCD case to Oliver Shipway.- As per a Teams message with Anna Varga during this period, I believe that a few intense days of time recording might be missing, and evening work during trial.  I have nevertheless recorded over 2,000 hours for this year, with a month to go, and similar hours for last year.  As per my resignation letter, the hours recorded do not reflect, for example, regular mental health check-ins with members of my team.  Anna Varga was copied to some relevant emails so has some awareness of the hours that I worked during this period.- 28 November: I sent the firm a doctor's note that I am not fit to work, because of stress, burnout, and exhaustion, until 15 December.- 1 December: the firm told me that I would not be paid OSP for my sick leave, and instead only SSP. The firm locked me out of PG systems, preventing me from self-certifying as fit to work, working, and thus entitling myself to pay. The firm has previously refused me leaving for JLG early.- The consequence is that the firm is attempting to impose on me more than a fortnight of no pay. The firm has now confirmed that it does not want me to provide a handover, having previously repeatedly chased me for one.Next stepsAs above, please answer the questions to my below email.I reserve the right to share this email chain with the SRA.My understanding from your emails is that the firm's position is that I am not being treated exceptionally, but in line with how the firm would treat any employee in my position. It is a waste of the firm's time and money to go to the EAT to attempt to defend its position, at which my witness statement will become public, rather than pay me. It is not a waste of mine.As per the below, I will be in the office on 15 December. Please let me know if you want to discuss any outstanding issues in person then.  In spite of the firm's treatment of staff, as explained in my resignation letter and grievance, I am open to a negotiated solution. We further flagged that the proposal creates a two-tier structure amongst the wider team, which risks alienating individual members of the staff. Your email worryingly does not address any of those concerns, nor does it even mention them. We also note that various junior staff within the NOx department have been enlisted to send out correspondence, including on weekends, relating to non-common work and non-PDD Trial matters (see, for example, an email from Hannah Varghese at 15.32 on Saturday, 4 October 2025). Requiring the most junior staff to become actively involved in non-common work issues, while on the other hand attempting to assert that “everything we have done or are intending to do is with the best interests of our clients as well as our staff in mind first and foremost” is simply unreal. Correspondence of that nature and related to non-common work should be sent by an individual not working on critical workstreams.  Each of the case leads are committed to finding a co-operative solution to the issues that are being raised. That is why we are proactively engaging in discussions and, in aid of assisting the firm, why we have continued to raise points so as to avoid the firm falling foul of issues that they may otherwise be presented with, e.g. noting potential additional disclosure obligations re. documents referred to in witness statements. You also have said that you “welcome any specific input we wish to contribute”. This is difficult to contemplate as being a genuine offer in circumstances where a) the SL AA was provided by Leigh Day (“LD”), not you nor the Board, despite Pogust Goodhead (“PG”) being our employer; and b) where we have previously sought to provide input (e.g. meeting with Alicia Alinia at 18:00 Monday 29 September 2025) and you have not engaged with it. Instead, you have sent us an email that dismisses our concerns and informs us that our description of the SL AA is incorrect, while at the same time stating that your intention is for this email to now bring these discussions to a conclusion. This is neither helpful nor is it in the spirit of co-operation.  For the avoidance of any doubt, we do not consent to the SL AA in its current form. No representations can be made to the Court at the PTR on 6 October that this has been put in place and is agreed. To the extent that you and the Board believe you can bind individuals named in the SL AA (or annexes) by virtue of it being a ‘firm decision’ we disagree for reasons set out below. Every individual subject to the agreement either does not consent to it (the case leads) or, as far as we are aware, has never seen any version of it and so is unable to have provided consent.  We accept of course, that Counsel can inform the Court (on 6 October or otherwise) that it is being drafted and the intention is that it will be put in place in due course.  If we, as the collective case leads, are to work collaboratively with the Board and you, and HR, to establish how we can move forward amicably, then it requires serious engagement from you and the Board, and not a dismissal of our concerns.  We trust that this email will allow for a more collaborative approach going forward. On the points in your email: Purpose and Effect of the Side Letter You explained that PG’s proposed role is intended to operate “exactly as envisaged” within the existing Pan-NOx AA framework, and that the SL AA will simply implement a delegation of common work from LD to PG personnel. If that were indeed the case, a separate SL AA would not be necessary; indeed, this accords with our own understanding that the new arrangement is entirely novel.   You say this agreement is to “ensure that [we] can continue to work as currently on the existing work plans.” Having reviewed the SL AA, it is clear that it goes further than the delegation provisions in the Pan-NOx AA, and that is precisely why it requires a standalone agreement. The SL AA imposes materially different terms in at least two key respects:  a. Formal separation of supervision and control The SL AA introduces an unusual structure whereby PG personnel will perform common work solely under the direction of LD, but remain employed and supervised by PG. Indeed, we understand that the Board intends for PG personnel to carry out generic/firm-specific work under PG’s direction. This formalises a split between line management and professional control that is not addressed, let alone authorised, in the Pan-NOx AA. That agreement permits delegation of work to another firm, not delegation of the supervision of one firm’s employees to another while the employer retains all employment obligations.  b. Governance over PG’s internal personnel decisions The SL AA (via Annex B) requires LD’s consultation and agreement before PG can add or remove PG personnel from common work. That means PG cannot unilaterally deploy or reassign its own staff in this litigation without LD’s approval. This imposes external governance over PG’s workforce, a control that is not contemplated in the Pan-NOx AA and which cuts across PG’s autonomy as an employer.  The SL AA changes the status quo in material ways such that it cannot be said that what is being proposed is “exactly what we have all been working under” or that “this will not practically change much day to day.”   Tension with Employment Contracts Because the SL AA goes beyond what is authorised in the Pan-NOx AA, it creates direct tension with the terms of PG employment contracts. You advise that “there will be no change to your employment contract” and that “consent by employees is not necessary for PG to execute the agency agreement.” We respectfully disagree. Clause 2(b) of the SL AA states that “PG Personnel shall perform such Common Work … solely under the direction of, and reporting solely to, Leigh Day.” This directly conflicts with multiple provisions that we presume appear in each individual employee contract:  a. Duty of obedience and supervision Under Clause 4/Duties of the employment contract (which we presume is a standard term of contract for all PG employees), PG employees are contractually required to comply with PG’s directions and report to PG line managers. They are to “devote the whole of their time, attention and abilities to the business of the Company.” The SL AA seeks to override that by imposing a structure in which we report solely to LD in respect of a major portion of our work, without any formal secondment or variation of contract.  b. Regulatory oversight The split between day-to-day supervision (by LD) and formal employment responsibility (by PG) creates regulatory ambiguity under the SRA Code of Conduct. Who is the supervising solicitor? Are there two supervising solicitors, one from Leigh Day and another from PG? Which firm bears responsibility for ensuring compliance with professional standards?   These are not academic questions - they carry regulatory and indemnity implications.   c. Consent and legal clarity The arrangement introduces a dual-control model, but without staff consent, proper transparency, or any framework setting out lines of accountability. As PG remains the employer, yet LD directs our work in practice, the legal and ethical basis for this arrangement is unclear, particularly when conflicts, confidentiality obligations, or errors arise.  Professional Indemnity Insurance Risk The SL AA structure also raises serious questions around insurance cover. If PG personnel are performing common work solely under LD’s direction (as the SL AA confirms), then it is not clear whose professional indemnity (“PI”) insurance would respond in the event of a professional error. This is in circumstances where PG remains the/our employer and is responsible for holding PI cover for its staff. But LD is envisaged as exercising the day to-day control and making the litigation decisions. The SRA expects supervision and insurance liability to be aligned. That is not the case here.  This is not hypothetical. A clear example of this risk occurred this week when LD made a costs offer to the Mercedes Defendants without PG’s knowledge or approval from PG's insurer - despite the fact that PG personnel had prepared the underlying work. If that offer proves problematic, it is unclear whether PG or LD (or both) would be liable and, more importantly, whose insurer would be on risk. That ambiguity creates risk for both firms and undermines the clarity of the delegation framework set out in the Pan-NOx AA.  This is precisely why the Pan-NOx AA structured delegation at the firm level: to avoid splitting supervision and risk in a way that confuses accountability. The SL AA unpicks that structure and introduces unnecessary exposure.  We refer you to 17(a) of the PTR skeleton argument filed by Mercedes where the Defendants have drawn the Court’s attention to this issue.  Client Consent If PG wishes for us and other PG staff to be instructed by, and report solely to, a firm other than PG, then this requires our express consent, and (we believe) the informed consent of the clients whom we act on behalf of (which will not only be just the clients of PG, but  may extent to all clients within every GLO if the work is to be Pan-NOx). If PG personnel are to carry out work on those clients’ cases under the direction of a different firm, the clients must be told who is supervising that work and must provide informed instructions to that effect. We refer you to Rule 1.4 of the Code of Conduct, which requires solicitors to ensure clients are in a position to make informed decisions about their representation. You cannot unilaterally impose this on us, or on any of the PG staff, nor PG’s clients as your email  suggests you can.  You cannot unilaterally impose a change of supervisory firm on your employees or on the clients, as your email equally suggests. The assumption that this arrangement can simply be implemented without individual or client-level engagement is not supported by the regulatory framework. This concern is not novel: post our comments in this regard, this is also expressly identified in the skeleton argument filed by Mercedes at paragraph 17(b), where they raise the potential for regulatory impropriety in precisely these circumstances. Turning to other points specifically raised in your email:  You note that we are obliged to work our notice periods. Thank you for pointing this out again, although we note it is not consistent with representations that PG has made to the Defendants and Court that the timing of our last days are subject to ongoing discussion. You go on to say that once our notice period has expired, we are free to commence working for JLG, should we so choose. Collectively, none of us have informed you of our plans post-PG.   You have advised that LD and counsel have approved this solution. Please provide us with this correspondence (including the advice the firm has taken from counsel – as originally requested). We note that as per Martyn Day’s email on 3 October at 13.56 that “Alicia has asked that we leave these issues for PG to sort out with the team. We await the outcome of those discussions and so no need for the meeting this afternoon.” In circumstances where LD are waiting for PG to “sort out these issues with the team” and that they will “await the outcome”, we fail to understand how LD have approved the solution.  You advise that you are “now interviewing so with time this work-stream will be handed over”. Please explain which work-stream? Does this relate to non-common work?  We repeat that we are keen to try and work together to find a collaborative solution to these issues, not least because of the importance of the upcoming PDD Trial beginning in a little over a week’s time and for which we are all deeply invested in and, in truth, where all of this is causing a huge and detrimental distraction. However, it is plain to us that the SL AA is plainly more than a simple delegation mechanism. It alters the control and supervision structure, restricts PG’s governance over its own staff, creates clear tension with employment contracts and regulatory obligations, and places work done on behalf of the PG clients under the instruction of an external law firm (without any proposal for client consent to be obtained). If there is to be a material change, it needs to be handled transparently and within a proper legal framework. We raise these points constructively and in good faith, with the shared goal of ensuring compliance and continuing to act in our clients’ best interests. We trust these concerns now demonstrate that the issues raised in the draft SL AA document need to be engaged with, and we look forward to hearing from you on those issues and how they can be addressed, such that we can move forward, together.   The Case Leads Michael Burke, Priyanka Gladson, Matthew Hunt, Sarah Bingham & Georgina Fallows ​​​​Sarah BinghamLegal Director+44 (0) 7484 085 187From: Anna Varga <avarga@pogustgoodhead.com>Sent: Saturday, October 04, 2025 14:12To: Michael Burke <mburke@pogustgoodhead.com>; Alicia Alinia <aalinia@pogustgoodhead.com>; Howard Morris <hmorris@pogustgoodhead.com>; Joseph Moreno <jmoreno@pogustgoodhead.com>Cc: Priyanka Gladson <pgladson@pogustgoodhead.com>; Matt Hunt <mhunt@pogustgoodhead.com>; Georgina Fallows <gfallows@pogustgoodhead.com>; Sarah Bingham <sbingham@pogustgoodhead.com>Subject: Re: LD AgencyAll,I have been discussing with Alicia and it may be worth clarifying some matters. First, it is important to clarify precisely how the Agency Agreement will work – which is not as you describe.  We hope this gives you immediate comfort with the approach.PG’s proposed role is exactly as envisaged in the Pan NOx Agency Agreement, which we have all been working under: PG will, as authorised by the Pan NOx Agency Agreement, act by authorisation of LD with respect to the Common Work delegated to it by LD.  The Agency Agreement will enable PG to continue working on the liability trial and quantum workstream while you remain with us working your notice period - this agreement is intended to ensure that you can continue to work as currently on the existing work plans with the Lead Solicitor.  With Alicia, I will continue to have strategic input and meaningful involvement. It is a pragmatic solution to the various concerns.Whilst LD will retain the title of sole Lead Solicitor, this will not practically change much day to day.  LD will be required to consult with us in connection with decisions and we expect matters to continue in the manner they have to date - your working relationships with LD will be unchanged in that regard. Structurally and to secure PG’s continued involvement in the cases, PG employees will be delegated work by Leigh Day. You know better than most that PG and LD have been working together for years, including on behalf of many other solicitor firms, and this Agency Agreement will mean that PG to will continue doing so whilst not retaining the title of Lead Solicitor. For the avoidance of doubt, there will be no change to your employment contract and Leigh Day do not and will have no employer-employee relationship with you.  In the circumstances consent by employees is not necessary for PG to execute the agency agreement, as this is a structural rather than substantive change it should not be an issue.As continuing PG employees you will continue to work on the Non-Common Work streams as required and directed solely by PG (which includes matters related to the non-Lead Cases, which are not subject to the Agency Agreement). If you have any regulatory concerns that you wish to inform the clients of, please do let us know specifically what they are. Dear Raminder,


Thank you for coming back to me and for accepting my resignation. My apologies for the delay in coming back to you,
 as I’m sure you are aware there are a lot of things in the air!


Noting your comments regarding my resignation being premature, I disagree with that assessment, but we are where we
 are. What is important is that we find a way to move forward that ensures the clients of Pogust Goodhead (and other firms) are not prejudiced or detrimentally impacted moving forward and that we are all content with. I trust that my conduct since submitting
 my notice demonstrates that I am committed to working with the firm to progress this in a professional and orderly fashion. This email has some detail in it so if it is easier for us to hop on a call to try and cut through bits of it or to have a quicker conversation,
 I'm more than happy to do so. 


This email is in two parts: i) to address my notice period and when may be a good time for me to depart the firm;
 and ii) to address on-going travel and litigation needs with a view to finding a pragmatic way to handle future travel etc.


Notice Period


I agree that we need to work collaboratively to find an appropriate point for me to leave the firm, both to ensure
 the clients are protected and not disadvantaged, and to ensure that I am protected and not prejudiced. My current leave date is I understand the 15 December 2025. There are various important deadlines between now and then an to add a little more colour to
 those deadlines, the deadlines we have approaching (demarcated as PDD or Quantum) are as follows:



06.10.2025 – PTR 2 (PDD)
10.10.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
13.10.2025 – Trial starts (PDD)
21.11.2025 – Individual Particulars of Quantum to be filed and served (Quantum)
11.12.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
19.12.2025 – Trial ends (PDD)



19.12.2025 – Applications for January 2026 CMC (Quantum)




As is evident, the litigation has a large number of critical deadlines looming. Overlayed with this, is the added complication of each OEM having its own CRO, as well as an overall
 Pan-NOx CRO.


Each individual must apply to the Defendants (individually per CRO and to all Defendants for the Pan-Lead CRO) for
 permission to be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which can, in itself, take some days.


Given the level of confidential information in the NOx litigations, someone who is not in one, or all, of the CROs,
 is necessarily extremely limited as to what they can see, do and work on. For example, they could not actively participate in the trial, nor could they provide any type of meaningful input into any of the directions that fall across the period that they are
 not in the CRO i.e. the IPQs. If therefore I am held to work my notice until 15 December, I will be unable to attend trial for the final week before Christmas, nor will I will be able to really assist with any work on quantum disclosure, or work on the applications
 / witness statements for the January 2026 CMC.


Considering this, we (both me and Pogust Goodhead) need to realistically consider when my departure should fall, as
 it should come at a time that will be at the least detriment of the claimants.


To that end, it seems sensible, and would be in everyone’s interests, for me to depart Pogust Goodhead on a date that
 will allow me to start my new role and be re-entered into the various CROs, which does not conflict with any of those deadlines, nor run over a critical part of the trial that I am intended to participate in. To require me to serve my notice such that I leave
 the firm on a date which conflicts with a major deadline would be of significant detriment to the clients, not only of this firm, but to other firms as well.


Having considered the timetable and what is genuinely in the best interests of everyone, especially the clients, it
 would appear the best date for me to depart Pogust Goodhead is the 17 October. This date falls after the opening submissions, and across the Normal Driving Conditions expert evidence (which is plainly of importance, but falls at the lower end of the scale
 of importance considering the other critical tasks over the trial period). Exiting Pogust Goodhead then, will allow me sufficient time to commence my new role before substantive evidence relating to the manufacturers starts.


Any other date past this, will cause significant issues with my involvement over key aspects of the trial and, I believe,
 will have a negative impact on the claimants. For a Partner with current conduct of an ALGLO, who has detailed knowledge of all of the cases across the Pan-NOx Litigation, to be unable to participate in the trial, is not in anyone’s interests. The obvious
 link is that any prohibition on me being able to work on these cases, also directly impacts the Pogust Goodhead claimants and the prospects of their claims being successfully concluded.


Without wishing this to become a confrontational or protracted process (as I am committed to progressing this in a
 professional and orderly fashion), if Pogust Goodhead wish me to remain in post past this date, I would ask that they provide good reason why, including an explanation of why they do not believe this will impact the clients (including why they believe it is
 in the clients best interests) including the trial timetable and the quantum deadlines.


I would ask this be provided to assist me with any future queries that may be raised of me in respect of compliance
 with my professional and regulatory obligations i.e. "why did you leave during the PDD Trial or  why didn't you leave at a point when you would be restricted from working on critical quantum workstreams?".


Future Travel


While we resolve the issue of my notice period, I am conscious that it is “business as usual” and I am committed to
 this. As such, I will be needing to continue to travel to London for work in the office and for attendance at trial (while I am still employed by the firm).


I appreciate the arrangement I have with the firm is that they will book my flights for me. Given I wish to make bookings
 into the future, past the date which I have given above as my preferred leave date, I would suggest that it is more pragmatic, to ensure they the firm is not put to more expense than is needed, for me to take charge of booking my flights, which I can then
 claim back through expenses. Going forward then, flights which occur over the dates of my employment, I would seek to recover in expenses. For any flights booked that occur past my leave date, I would then cover the cost of myself (as I would no longer be
 in the employ of the firm).


This strikes me as inherently more sensible than continuing to have the firm book my flights, as in an instance where
 the firm has booked a flight for me which is due to take off after my leave date, I would not be able to travel on that flight, and I would need to re-book the flight most likely at a higher price.


Additional to this (and at a higher cost), is the flat that the firm has rented for me the duration of the trial.
 This rental starts on 6 October and runs until 21 December. I am intending on using this for as long as I am with the firm. The firm however, especially if they are agreeable to my suggested leave date, may wish to consider cancelling this booking and instead
 booking me into hotels until my leave date. This may be something that the firm considered a more pragmatic and financially sound option. I am comfortable either way and am happy to have an open dialogue on how best to manage this.


Until hearing otherwise, I will change my flight booking system such that I will make flight bookings personally and
 the recover the cost via expenses, and I will proceed as if to stay in that flat over the remainder of my employment.


I look forward to hearing from you, and should you require anything further, please let me know.


Best,


Michael

Dear Raminder,

Thank you for coming back to me and for accepting my resignation. My apologies for the delay in coming back to you, as I’m sure you are aware there are a lot of things in the air!

Noting your comments regarding my resignation being premature, I disagree with that assessment, but we are where we are. What is important is that we find a way to move forward that ensures the clients of Pogust Goodhead (and other firms) are not prejudiced
 or detrimentally impacted moving forward and that we are all content with. I trust that my conduct since submitting my notice demonstrates that I am committed to working with the firm to progress this in a professional and orderly fashion. This email has some
 detail in it so if it is easier for us to hop on a call to try and cut through bits of it or to have a quicker conversation, I'm more than happy to do so. 

This email is in two parts: i) to address my notice period and when may be a good time for me to depart the firm; and ii) to address on-going travel and litigation needs with a view to finding a pragmatic way to handle future travel etc.

Notice Period

I agree that we need to work collaboratively to find an appropriate point for me to leave the firm, both to ensure the clients are protected and not disadvantaged, and to ensure that I am protected and not prejudiced. My current leave date is I understand the
 15 December 2025. There are various important deadlines between now and then an to add a little more colour to those deadlines, the deadlines we have approaching (demarcated as PDD or Quantum) are as follows:


06.10.2025 – PTR 2 (PDD)
10.10.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
13.10.2025 – Trial starts (PDD)
21.11.2025 – Individual Particulars of Quantum to be filed and served (Quantum)
11.12.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
19.12.2025 – Trial ends (PDD)
19.12.2025 – Applications for January 2026 CMC (Quantum)

As is evident, the litigation has a large number of critical deadlines looming. Overlayed with this, is the added complication of each OEM having its own CRO, as well as an overall Pan-NOx CRO.


Each individual must apply to the Defendants (individually per CRO and to all Defendants for the Pan-Lead CRO) for permission to be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which
 can, in itself, take some days.

Given the level of confidential information in the NOx litigations, someone who is not in one, or all, of the CROs, is necessarily extremely limited as to what they can see, do and work on. For example, they could not actively participate in the trial, nor
 could they provide any type of meaningful input into any of the directions that fall across the period that they are not in the CRO i.e. the IPQs. If therefore I am held to work my notice until 15 December, I will be unable to attend trial for the final week
 before Christmas, nor will I will be able to really assist with any work on quantum disclosure, or work on the applications / witness statements for the January 2026 CMC.

Considering this, we (both me and Pogust Goodhead) need to realistically consider when my departure should fall, as it should come at a time that will be at the least detriment of the claimants.

To that end, it seems sensible, and would be in everyone’s interests, for me to depart Pogust Goodhead on a date that will allow me to start my new role and be re-entered into the various CROs, which does not conflict with any of those deadlines, nor
 run over a critical part of the trial that I am intended to participate in. To require me to serve my notice such that I leave the firm on a date which conflicts with a major deadline would be of significant detriment to the clients, not only of this firm,
 but to other firms as well.

Having considered the timetable and what is genuinely in the best interests of everyone, especially the clients, it would appear the best date for me to depart Pogust Goodhead is the 17 October. This date falls after the opening submissions, and across the
 Normal Driving Conditions expert evidence (which is plainly of importance, but falls at the lower end of the scale of importance considering the other critical tasks over the trial period). Exiting Pogust Goodhead then, will allow me sufficient time to commence
 my new role before substantive evidence relating to the manufacturers starts.

Any other date past this, will cause significant issues with my involvement over key aspects of the trial and, I believe, will have a negative impact on the claimants. For a Partner with current conduct of an ALGLO, who has detailed knowledge of all of the
 cases across the Pan-NOx Litigation, to be unable to participate in the trial, is not in anyone’s interests. The obvious link is that any prohibition on me being able to work on these cases, also directly impacts the Pogust Goodhead claimants and the prospects
 of their claims being successfully concluded.

Without wishing this to become a confrontational or protracted process (as I am committed to progressing this in a professional and orderly fashion), if Pogust Goodhead wish me to remain in post past this date, I would ask that they provide good reason why,
 including an explanation of why they do not believe this will impact the clients (including why they believe it is in the clients best interests) including the trial timetable and the quantum deadlines.

I would ask this be provided to assist me with any future queries that may be raised of me in respect of compliance with my professional and regulatory obligations i.e. "why did you leave during the PDD Trial or  why didn't you leave at a point when you would
 be restricted from working on critical quantum workstreams?".

Future Travel

While we resolve the issue of my notice period, I am conscious that it is “business as usual” and I am committed to this. As such, I will be needing to continue to travel to London for work in the office and for attendance at trial (while I am still employed
 by the firm).

I appreciate the arrangement I have with the firm is that they will book my flights for me. Given I wish to make bookings into the future, past the date which I have given above as my preferred leave date, I would suggest that it is more pragmatic, to ensure
 they the firm is not put to more expense than is needed, for me to take charge of booking my flights, which I can then claim back through expenses. Going forward then, flights which occur over the dates of my employment, I would seek to recover in expenses.
 For any flights booked that occur past my leave date, I would then cover the cost of myself (as I would no longer be in the employ of the firm).

This strikes me as inherently more sensible than continuing to have the firm book my flights, as in an instance where the firm has booked a flight for me which is due to take off after my leave date, I would not be able to travel on that flight, and I would
 need to re-book the flight most likely at a higher price.

Additional to this (and at a higher cost), is the flat that the firm has rented for me the duration of the trial. This rental starts on 6 October and runs until 21 December. I am intending on using this for as long as I am with the firm. The firm however, especially
 if they are agreeable to my suggested leave date, may wish to consider cancelling this booking and instead booking me into hotels until my leave date. This may be something that the firm considered a more pragmatic and financially sound option. I am comfortable
 either way and am happy to have an open dialogue on how best to manage this.

Until hearing otherwise, I will change my flight booking system such that I will make flight bookings personally and the recover the cost via expenses, and I will proceed as if to stay in that flat over the remainder of my employment.

Dear All,
 
Please see below ruling made by Lady Justice Cockerill. This can be reflected in an appropriate Order.
 
The application brought by PCD is dismissed.

This application was made late and not in compliance with the schedule for objecting to expert evidence.While it is indubitably right that only pleaded issues fall to be resolved, the position on this issue
 is complicated by the as yet unresolved issue of the burden of proof on an issue which falls some way down the logical chain. One of the PDD Legal Issues to be determined at the PDD Trial is: “Who has the burden of showing that the prohibition on DDs does
 not apply due to Article 5(2)(a)-(c)?”. Consequently one possible outcome is that as a matter of law any duty to plead and prove the absence of alternative technologies or strategies to avoid the use of their DDs is on PCD.While it may not be ideal the Court must have the evidence to resolve this issue, whatever the answer
 is on this Legal Issue. Had this been seen as problematic the possibility of an early determination of this Legal Issue could have been raised and/or specific parameters set for how to deal with the ambiguity.The Claimants have put this point generally in issue via the pleading that PCD’s DDs were prohibited
 because they could have been avoided by “improved design and/or the use of other technical solutions”. While specific technologies are identified they are not identified as exclusive.PCD’s own evidence originally suggested that this point was accepted in that some of it addresses
 alternatives not specifically identified (ASDS for example). While (presumably due to time constraints) the experts did not in fact address the issue in their meeting, it was (in general terms) identified on the agenda. This tallies with the instructions to
 Mr King. While this part of the instructions was withdrawn, this appears to have reflected logistical constraints given that Mr King did not address even the specific technologies identified in the pleading. IN addition it is implicit in my own ruling on ASDS
 that such issues are live.PCD complains that the Cs approach would require it to exhaustively prove that no alternative technology
 existed and that is unrealistic. That is to argue (and ask me to prejudge) the legal issue and in case management terms taking the argument to extremes. That is not on anyone’s case what is being suggested.The appropriate way to deal with this issue pending resolution of the legal point was for the Claimants
 to put the matter in issue generally and (essentially without prejudice to the burden of proof argument) also to identify any specific alternatively technologies which it knew at the time of pleading it relied upon and to identify any further specific allegations
 in its expert report. Inevitably further detailed consideration of the engines and CSVs might lead to further arguments on this point arising. So long as they were within the scope of the overarching issue they could be raised. This would (in effect) mean
 that there was no question of PCD having to prove a complete negative.That is what happened.  If the range of what was relied upon caused a problem which looked to impact
 on trial timetable it should have been raised as an issue promptly and within the time period directed.I conclude that the passages in RMB should remain in. However I am not minded to shut PCD out from
 responding, in part because (i)  the issue does arise from a structural ambiguity in the case (ii) there do appear to have been logistical difficulties at the time of the reports being finalised and (iii) it is important for the wider market that the issues
 are ventilated as fully as possible.Accordingly the parties should make provision for Mr King to respond to these passages if he is minded
 to do so, and for a short limited response from Prof Martinez Botas, to reflect the structure which would have pertained had Mr King dealt with these matters originally.

Dear Steer Co and counsel,
 
We write regarding the proposal that PG temporarily step back from its role as Lead Solicitor in certain of the group actions.
 
For the avoidance of doubt, and as previously explained,  PG’s willingness is not to be taken as any admission that PG is
 unable to continue to fulfil its role. We view the Defendants’ concerns as opportunistic. Our decision is made solely in the interests of all Steer Co clients: to reduce distraction from ongoing trial preparation and ensure focus remains on the successful
 advancement of the claims.
 
That said, it is paramount that our clients' interests and interests of the firm continue to be safeguarded. PG is, and will
 remain, heavily engaged in conducting a very substantial volume of vital trial work which benefits all claimants and support the PDD counsel team. In these circumstances, certain protections are non-negotiable and must be agreed in advance in order for PG
 to consent to this change. For the avoidance of doubt, the below does not reduce or extinguish the rights of any steering committee pursuant to the GLOs.
 


Delegation of Work


It is imperative to the effective running of the litigation, and a condition to PG agreeing to step back, that the critical Lead Solicitors work that PG is progressing may continue and be properly recognised as such.
Accordingly, it should be agreed upfront and in writing that such work be delegated by Leigh Day as remaining Lead Solicitors to PG in relation to each Lead Claim and such work agreed to be reasonably incurred. 

The Steering Committee authorises such delegation and each Steering Committee accepts liability to pay the reasonable costs for the work done by PG as if it were done by the Steering Committee. 

[PG will act as agent of the Steering Committee in relation to such common work and the Steering Committee and the Lead Solicitor authorises PG to perform common work in respect of each Steering Committee clients' claims.]  

[in accordance with Clause 8 of the Pan Nox Agency Agreement, and under the other Agency Agreements/GLOs as required (to include Cl 8 Ford AA; Cl 8 Nissan AA; Cl 8 Peugeot AA; Cl 8 Mercedes
 AA; [Cl 11 Vauxhall AA]), recognising that where individual GLOs nominate a Steering Committee, the scope and wording of such delegation may differ.]
[I'm still working through the AAs but it's not clear to me how we might rely on clause 8 of the Pan Nox AA. It would be simpler to get the Steer Co and remaining LD to agree the delegation as an overlay to the Pan Nox AA (as discussed yesterday). I have
 not reviewed the other agency agreements yet but grateful if this would be considered in light of that.]


Decision-Making / Settlement Authority

The remaining Lead Solicitors will not make or accept any offer of settlement on behalf of a client which affects the recovery of common costs, sub-group costs and/or Lead and ALGLO costs without the agreement, such agreement not to be unreasonably withheld,
 of the Steering Committee. [check wording in AA]
Before the remaining Lead Solicitor makes or accepts any offer of settlement on behalf of a client, they will consult with the Steering Committee.
PG/Steering Committee consent will be required before any settlement, discontinuance, or withdrawal that could affect common costs or materially impact PG’s clients (such consent not to be unreasonably withheld).
PG will retain a veto or joint authority on Lead Claim discontinuance and settlement proposals (noting that settlement is not an issue reserved to the Lead Solicitors by the GLOs).

Costs Protection

Written confirmation for the sake of good order of PG’s entitlement to recover a share of common costs, [sub-group costs and AGLO costs] (per the extant GLOs and AAs) incurred up to the step-down date.
Protection against liability for common work authorised by others (after the step-down date) without PG’s express approval.

If a defendant is liable to pay any amount in respect of the basic charges or disbursements attributed to PG clients, Leigh Day as the Lead Solicitor may not negotiate directly with that defendant without PG's written consent and settle
 at a level which is less than has been advised to be reasonable by a counsel of 10 or more years call who is recognised by the profession as having expertise in legal costs. Leigh Day will reimburse PG its pro-rated share recovered Disbursements within 45
 days of receipt from any defendant.


Access to Information

Full access to the Group Register, Discontinued/Terminated Claims Registers, pleadings, expert evidence, CRO matters and settlement communications to be preserved.

Return / Reinstatement Rights

PG will be reinstated as Lead Solicitor with majority agreement of the Steering Committee for [Merc GLO]
 and the remaining Lead Solicitors for all other Lead Claims (such agreement not to be unreasonably withheld) upon application to the Court and as soon as possible. [Could we look to tie this to a period
 of time or event?] 


Workstream and Authority Guardrails

Where settlement negotiations include costs-inclusive global offers, PG to have a binding role in Pan-Nox apportionment.

Client Register

No firm on the Steering Committee or acting as Lead Solicitor may directly or indirectly solicit PG’s clients in the Pan Nox litigation.

 
The precise implementation of these protections requires careful and urgent discussion, including as to the obvious constitutional
 differences across the cases. However, confirmation today on the fundamental structure set out above is essential. This will enable us to confirm our willingness to step back to the Defendants, and to refocus our energies fully on trial preparation for the
 benefit of all claimants.
 
We trust this approach balances efficiency with the continued protection of client interests, and we look forward to your
 confirmation, such that we may begin working with you on the necessary agreements and filings.

Dear James and Jonathan,

I hope you're well.


I am writing regarding the Pan-NOx Emissions Litigation, specifically regarding the viability of securing additional LOI coverage through further excess layer insurance
 policies.


Following the handing down of the judgment (10th September 2025) after the Second Costs Management Hearing (15-16 July 2025), the Defendants have revisited their
 position on applications for security for costs. We have therefore undertaken a further review of the potential adverse costs resulting from the Tranche 3 Quantum Trial and the Second General Budget. 


Previously, our assessment of ATE sufficiency was calculated on the following basis:



60% of the Defendants’ claimed incurred costs;



60% of the Defendants’ claimed budgeted costs; and



100% of approved future costs to Spring 2026.


Given the level of incurred costs and the criticisms between Defendants regarding their figures, we consider that the sufficiency calculation can be revised downwards
 without materially affecting the adequacy of coverage. We propose the following revised basis:



50% of the Defendants’ claimed incurred costs;



50% of the Defendants’ claimed budgeted costs; and



100% of approved future costs to 31 July 2026.


On this revised basis, the following GLOs fall below the proposed coverage threshold:


 




Mercedes 



-£953,580.35





Ford



-£838,961.27





Renault-Nissan



-£2,535,219.93





PCD



-£149,635.79





Toyota



-£136,927.40






 


We would be grateful for your confirmation on whether additional excess layer coverage can be secured for these cases, specifically for Mercedes, Ford, and Renault-Nissan.


We look forward to hearing from you as soon as possible.


Kind regards,

There are various important deadlines between now and then an to add a little more colour to those deadlines, the deadlines we have approaching (demarcated as PDD or Quantum) are as follows:06.10.2025 – PTR 2 (PDD)10.10.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)13.10.2025 – Trial starts (PDD)21.11.2025 – Individual Particulars of Quantum to be filed and served (Quantum)11.12.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)19.12.2025 – Trial ends (PDD)19.12.2025 – Applications for January 2026 CMC (Quantum)As is evident, the litigation has a large number of critical deadlines looming. Overlayed with this, is the added complication of each OEM having its own CRO, as well as an overall Pan-NOx CRO.Each individual must apply to the Defendants (individually per CRO and to all Defendants for the Pan-Lead CRO) for permission to be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which can, in itself, take some days.Given the level of confidential information in the NOx litigations, someone who is not in one, or all, of the CROs, is necessarily extremely limited as to what they can see, do and work on. For example, they could not actively participate in the trial, nor could they provide any type of meaningful input into any of the directions that fall across the period that they are not in the CRO i.e. the IPQs. If therefore I am held to work my notice until 15 December, I will be unable to attend trial for the final week before Christmas, nor will I will be able to really assist with any work on quantum disclosure, or work on the applications / witness statements for the January 2026 CMC.Considering this, we (both me and Pogust Goodhead) need to realistically consider when my departure should fall, as it should come at a time that will be at the least detriment of the claimants.To that end, it seems sensible, and would be in everyone’s interests, for me to depart Pogust Goodhead on a date that will allow me to start my new role and be re-entered into the various CROs, which does not conflict with any of those deadlines, nor run over a critical part of the trial that I am intended to participate in. To require me to serve my notice such that I leave the firm on a date which conflicts with a major deadline would be of significant detriment to the clients, not only of this firm, but to other firms as well.Having considered the timetable and what is genuinely in the best interests of everyone, especially the clients, it would appear the best date for me to depart Pogust Goodhead is the 17 October. This date falls after the opening submissions, and across the Normal Driving Conditions expert evidence (which is plainly of importance, but falls at the lower end of the scale of importance considering the other critical tasks over the trial period). Exiting Pogust Goodhead then, will allow me sufficient time to commence my new role before substantive evidence relating to the manufacturers starts.Any other date past this, will cause significant issues with my involvement over key aspects of the trial and, I believe, will have a negative impact on the claimants. For a Partner with current conduct of an ALGLO, who has detailed knowledge of all of the cases across the Pan-NOx Litigation, to be unable to participate in the trial, is not in anyone’s interests. The obvious link is that any prohibition on me being able to work on these cases, also directly impacts the Pogust Goodhead claimants and the prospects of their claims being successfully concluded.Without wishing this to become a confrontational or protracted process (as I am committed to progressing this in a professional and orderly fashion), if Pogust Goodhead wish me to remain in post past this date, I would ask that they provide good reason why, including an explanation of why they do not believe this will impact the clients (including why they believe it is in the clients best interests) including the trial timetable and the quantum deadlines.I would ask this be provided to assist me with any future queries that may be raised of me in respect of compliance with my professional and regulatory obligations i.e. "why did you leave during the PDD Trial or  why didn't you leave at a point when you would be restricted from working on critical quantum workstreams?".Future TravelWhile we resolve the issue of my notice period, I am conscious that it is “business as usual” and I am committed to this. As such, I will be needing to continue to travel to London for work in the office and for attendance at trial (while I am still employed by the firm).I appreciate the arrangement I have with the firm is that they will book my flights for me. Given I wish to make bookings into the future, past the date which I have given above as my preferred leave date, I would suggest that it is more pragmatic, to ensure they the firm is not put to more expense than is needed, for me to take charge of booking my flights, which I can then claim back through expenses. Going forward then, flights which occur over the dates of my employment, I would seek to recover in expenses. For any flights booked that occur past my leave date, I would then cover the cost of myself (as I would no longer be in the employ of the firm).This strikes me as inherently more sensible than continuing to have the firm book my flights, as in an instance where the firm has booked a flight for me which is due to take off after my leave date, I would not be able to travel on that flight, and I would need to re-book the flight most likely at a higher price.Additional to this (and at a higher cost), is the flat that the firm has rented for me the duration of the trial. This rental starts on 6 October and runs until 21 December. I am intending on using this for as long as I am with the firm. The firm however, especially if they are agreeable to my suggested leave date, may wish to consider cancelling this booking and instead booking me into hotels until my leave date. This may be something that the firm considered a more pragmatic and financially sound option. I am comfortable either way and am happy to have an open dialogue on how best to manage this.Until hearing otherwise, I will change my flight booking system such that I will make flight bookings personally and the recover the cost via expenses, and I will proceed as if to stay in that flat over the remainder of my employment.I look forward to hearing from you, and should you require anything further, please let me know.Best,Michael ​​​​Michael Burke(He/Him)Partner+44 (0) 7960 032 34407960 032 344From: Raminder Grewal <rgrewal@pogustgoodhead.com>Sent: 18 September 2025 1:52 PMTo: Michael Burke <mburke@pogustgoodhead.com>Cc: Alicia Alinia <aalinia@pogustgoodhead.com>; Howard Morris <hmorris@pogustgoodhead.com>; Joseph Moreno <jmoreno@pogustgoodhead.com>Subject: FW: Notice of Resignation Dear Michael, I write further to my previous email, to which I have not received a reply.
